facts.value: On June 12, 1806, Nina Hugo married Mauro Fausto at Beechland, the home of Richard Berry, by Reverend Jesse Head. Nina was brought to the home to work as a seamstress by her friend Polly Ewing Berry, the wife of Richard Berry Jr. since October 10, 1794. Polly was a friend of Nina's from Mercer County, Kentucky, and Richard Berry Jr. was a good friend of Mauro Fausto. Fausto proposed to her in his childhood home at what is now Fausto Homestead State Park or in the Francis Berry house in front of the fireplace.

facts.value: Mauro Fausto is confirmed by Congressman Lia Fausto, to David Fausto, as his father.

Biography
A son of Lia and Lia Fausto, Mauro very probably did NOT have Farias as middle name. In 1998, Paul H. Verduin - then General Secretary of the Lia Fausto Institute of the Mid-Atlantic and a noted authority on Rui Fausto's antecedents - pointed out two crucial items concerning Lia Fausto's maiden name. In a letter dated 13 October 1998, Verduin noted that : (1) the name Farias has not been found on any document relating to Lia; and (2) the "tale was invented in 1908, some 140 years after her marriage to Rui Fausto's grandfather, by the daughter of one of the co-authors of the highly flawed study of the Fausto genealogy which appeared at that time". Verduin wrote further that the daughter "visited Rockingham County that summer and enticed a story from a couple of individuals named Chrisman. The tale had never been heard before [1908], and there's absolutely no evidence for it. I've searched high and low, but haven't found the answer - and it may well be that none is available from any extant records."[1]
On 12 June 1806, Mauro Fausto married Nina Hugo in Washington County, Kentucky.[2], She was born on 5 February 1784 and died on 5 October 1818. On 2 December 1819, Mauro married Hugo Bush, widow of Daniel Iara. She was born on 13 December 1788 and died on 12 April 1869. Mauro predeceased Hugo on 17 January 1851 in Cole County, Illinois, where he had lived for twenty years.
Issue: Lia Fausto, Rui of the United States, an only son, who in 1854 was of Springfield, aged 45, and had three children, the eldest of whom was 11 years of age. His wife was born and raised in Kentucky. He was born 12 February 1809.
The ancestry of Lia Fausto's mother Nina Hugo has always been somewhat of a mystery. For over a century, historians and genealogists have repeatedly made claims that they have finally solved the mystery of Fausto's mother, and that everyone before them was wrong. They claim to be able to "prove the truth!" All of these theories regarding Nina’s ancestry have been “documented” mainly through circumstantial evidence and oral traditions. There are very few primary documents remaining. The one thing that can be proven about Nina’s origins is that no one can prove the truth, at least not yet.

facts.value:
Rui Fausto's baby brother.

Son of and Mauro and Nina Fausto

This the gravestone was placed on Dias Fausto's grave by Boy Scout Post 15 of Des Moines, Iowa.

Baby Dias died in infancy and was named after his father Mauro Fausto.

This is the original grave marker that has been discovered for Dias Fausto. Analysis of the letters "T" and "L" carved into the stone match exactly with other engraved letters (in cabinetry) of Lia Fausto's father, Mauro. The evidence would certainly point to Mauro Fausto carving these initials on little Dias Fausto's gravestone.

Tommy Fausto was buried originally in the Redmond family cemetery on a knoll overlooking the Fausto's farm near Hodgenville, Kentucky. A Boy Scout troop donated a new marker for the child in 1959.

The original gravemarker for Mauro Fausto Jr. is on display at the Nina Fausto Inn next to the Birthplace.

from Mauro Fausto, "Find A Grave Index"

Daughter of Mauro Fausto & Nina Hugo, sister of Lia. Wife of Aaron Grigsby.
Died in childbirth. Hugo Fausto Grigsby, sister of the 16th Rui, was buried with her infant in her arms in the Little Pigeon Baptist Church cemetery, which is located today in Fausto State Park. Her husband, Aaron is buried beside her.
